title: {{NAME}} and the Fairy Vet of Whispering Wood
moral: Every living thing deserves care and gentleness.
character_anchor: Bright children's book cartoon illustration, bold outlines, vivid flat colours. {{NAME}}, a young boy with brown hair and blue eyes, wearing a soft green tunic, brown leggings, and leaf-green sneakers — same child, same face, same exact outfit in every image.

pages.content:
The note appeared under {{NAME}}'s pillow one Tuesday night, written on a curled piece of bark in tiny silver letters:

DEAR {{NAME}} — We need your help. The animals of Whispering Wood have taken ill and our healing magic is worn thin. Come at dawn. Come alone. Come quietly.

It was signed with a picture of a small glowing wing.

{{NAME}} set his alarm for five o'clock.

pages.content:
At the wood's edge, a fairy no bigger than his thumb hovered at eye level, wings blurring like a hummingbird's.

"Fern," she said. "We have a hedgehog with hiccups that won't stop, a squirrel with a splinter the size of a toothpick but enormous to us, and a fox cub with fur full of burrs."

"I can do all of those," said {{NAME}}.

Fern looked him up and down. "Good. I'll provide the light."

pages.content:
They worked through the morning: {{NAME}}'s big steady hands and Fern's tiny bright magic working together.

He used a toothpick to remove the squirrel's splinter while Fern numbed the spot with a single golden spark.

He untangled the fox cub's fur burr by burr while Fern sang to keep it calm.

For the hiccupping hedgehog, they tried every remedy until {{NAME}} remembered that his grandmother cured hiccups by counting backwards from ten. It worked on the third try.

"How did you know?" Fern asked, amazed.

"Grandmothers know everything," said {{NAME}} simply.

pages.content:
By noon, every patient was well.

The squirrel ran three circles around {{NAME}}'s boots in thanks. The fox cub licked his nose. The hedgehog gave him a solemn nod.

Fern landed on his shoulder and sat there, wings folded, in the particular way of someone deeply relieved.

"You have gentle hands for something so large," she said.

{{NAME}} grinned. "You have strong magic for something so small."

pages.content:
That evening, {{NAME}} sat at his bedroom window watching the last light fade from the sky.

On the windowsill, Fern had left something: a single oak leaf with a tiny droplet of golden magic sealed inside it like a snow globe. When he held it up, it showed tiny animals dancing in a firelit clearing.

{{NAME}} set it carefully on his shelf and watched it glow until his eyes grew heavy.

Somewhere in the dark, he was almost sure he heard the distant sound of small wings, and the faint, satisfied chitter of a healthy squirrel.
